note: Time-of-day greetings take the plural -lar/-ler: iyi akşamlar, iyi geceler, iyi günler. Note the dotted capital İ, which Turkish keeps distinct from dotless I.
Said when parting at night or going to bed; 'gece' is night. For arriving in the evening use 'iyi akşamlar' instead.
'Hoş' (pleasant) is a Persian loan; 'geldiniz' is the past tense of gelmek in the polite/plural form. The expected reply is 'Hoş bulduk'.
The fixed answer to 'hoş geldin(iz)'. Always in the 'we' form (-k), even when one person is speaking.
'Nasıl' (how) + the personal ending -sınız. The informal singular is 'Nasılsın?'. Turkish attaches 'to be' as a suffix, so no separate verb is needed.
'İyi' (good) + -im (I am). Because 'iyi' ends in a vowel, the buffer consonant -y- is inserted before the ending. Usually followed by 'teşekkürler, siz?'.
'Afiyet' (health, well-being) is Arabic; 'olsun' is the optative of olmak (to be). Said before, during and after a meal, and also as a reply when someone thanks the cook.
'Özür' (excuse, apology) comes from Arabic 'ʿudhr'; 'dilerim' is 'I wish/request' from dilemek. More formal than 'pardon'.
A French loan, used for minor apologies and to get past someone. Spelled as in French but pronounced with Turkish vowels.
'Rica' (request) is Arabic 'rajāʾ' + the helper verb etmek. Literally 'I beg (you not to mention it)'. Also used to mean 'please do' when granting a favour.
'Değil' is the negative of 'to be' for nouns and adjectives. A casual reply to thanks; 'ne demek' (what does it mean) is another.
'Sağ' means 'right (side)' but also 'alive, healthy'. 'Sağ olun' is the polite form. Also used to say 'bless you' for help received.
From görmek (to see) with the reciprocal suffix -üş- (görüşmek = to meet, see each other) and the aorist 'we' ending -ürüz.
'Memnun' (pleased) is an Arabic participle; 'oldum' is the past of olmak. The reply is 'Ben de' (me too).
Native Turkish. Colloquially people also say 'he' or 'hı hı', and 'tabii' (of course) for an enthusiastic yes.
From Arabic 'khayr' (good), originally a polite softener. The same word 'hayır' also means 'charity, good deed'. In casual speech 'yok' (there isn't) often replaces it.
From Arabic 'tamām' (complete, whole). Extremely common; 'Tamam mı?' asks 'OK?'.

en: Here you are / go ahead / come in
note: Imperative of buyurmak (to deign, to command). An all-purpose polite word: handing something over, inviting someone in, or asking 'how can I help?'.
'El' (hand) + -iniz (your) + dative -e; 'sağlık' is health. Said to whoever cooked or made something by hand. Informal: 'eline sağlık'.
'Geçmiş' is the past participle of geçmek (to pass); 'olsun' means 'may it be'. Said after illness, an accident or any unpleasant experience.
'Kusur' (fault, flaw) is Arabic; 'bakma' is the negative imperative of bakmak (to look). Polite form: 'kusura bakmayın'.

en: Good day / have a nice day
note: Used both as a daytime greeting and when leaving a shop. Like other time greetings it uses the plural 'günler'.
From Arabic 'salām' (peace). Casual among friends; the fuller 'selamünaleyküm' is the religious greeting.
'Efendi' (master, sir) + -m (my). Used to answer when someone calls your name, to ask them to repeat, and to answer the phone.
'Tebrik' is Arabic; the plural -ler makes it an exclamation. The verb is 'tebrik etmek' (to congratulate).
From Arabic 'ṣifr' (empty), the same source as English 'cipher' and 'zero'. Note the dotless ı in both syllables.
Also the indefinite article 'a/an': 'bir çay' = a tea. Nouns after numbers stay singular: 'iki çay', not 'iki çaylar'.
Native Turkic. 'İkisi de' means 'both of them'.
Pronounced 'ooch' with rounded lips; the ç is always 'ch' in Turkish.
'Dördüncü' (fourth) shows the final t softening to d before a vowel suffix.
Native Turkic. 'Beşinci' is fifth.
Identical in spelling to 'altı' meaning 'its underside' (alt + -ı), so context decides.
Also the past tense of yemek: 'yedi' = he/she ate. Stress and context tell them apart.
Native Turkic. 'Sekizinci' is eighth.
Native Turkic; 'dokuzuncu' is ninth, with the vowel of -(ı)ncı harmonising to u.
11-19 are simply 'on' + the unit: on bir, on iki, on üç ... on dokuz. Written as two words.
Compound numbers are written as separate words: on bir, yirmi beş, yüz on iki. (Only on cheques are they joined.)
Native Turkic. 'Yirmi bir' = 21, and so on up to 'yirmi dokuz'.
Native Turkic. Tens are not built from the units in Turkish: each of 20-90 is its own word.
Forty is a symbolic 'many' in Turkish idiom: 'kırk yılda bir' = once in a blue moon (once in forty years).
Looks like 'el' (hand) + -li, but is simply the native word for fifty.
Related to 'altı' (six) but with the vowel dropped: alt-mış. Not a regular formation.
Related to 'yedi' (seven) with d becoming t. Identical in form to 'yetmiş' (it has sufficed, from yetmek).
Historically 'sekiz on' (eight tens) contracted; 'doksan' (ninety) was formed the same way.
Historically 'dokuz on' (nine tens) contracted.
No 'one' before it: 'yüz' = 100, 'iki yüz' = 200. The same word means 'face', and 'yüzmek' is 'to swim'.
'Bin' = 1000, 'iki bin' = 2000. Also the imperative of binmek (to get on a vehicle).
Ordinals add -(i)nci with vowel harmony: birinci, ikinci, üçüncü, dördüncü, beşinci. Written '1.' with a full stop.
'Yarım' is half on its own (yarım ekmek = half a loaf). After a number use 'buçuk': 'bir buçuk' = one and a half.
From Persian 'juft'. 'Bir çift ayakkabı' = a pair of shoes; 'çift' also means a couple (two people) and 'even' (number). 'Çiftçi' is a farmer.
From Arabic 'ʿāʾila'. 'Ailem' = my family; 'aile' takes front-vowel suffixes because its last vowel is e.
'Annem' = my mother. The older word 'ana' survives in compounds like 'anayasa' (constitution) and 'anadil' (mother tongue).
'Babam' = my father. Also a respectful title for an old man or a saint, as in Baba Mountain names.
From 'karın' (belly, womb) + -daş (fellow). Gender-neutral; add 'kız' or 'erkek' for sister/brother. Also used warmly for friends.
Turkish distinguishes older from younger siblings. 'Abla' is also a polite way to address any slightly older woman.
Written 'ağabey' (ağa + bey) but pronounced and often written 'abi'. Used to address older men informally, like 'bro' or 'sir'.

example.en: Bro, can I get the bill?

note: Plural 'çocuklar'. Final k softens before a vowel suffix: 'çocuğum' (my child).
The vowel drops when a suffix is added: 'oğlum' (my son), 'oğlu' (his son). 'Oğlum' is also a common affectionate address to a boy.
Means both 'girl' and 'daughter'. 'Kızım' = my daughter, also used by elders to address any girl. 'Kız kardeş' = sister.
Used for 'male' with people and animals ('erkek kedi' = tom cat). 'Adam' is the usual word for 'a man' as a person.
Turkish nouns have no grammatical gender; 'kadın' and 'erkek' are simply separate words. 'Kadınlar' = women.
Historically the plural of 'oğul' (son). Today 'erkek çocuk' is more neutral; 'oğlan' can sound rustic.
Used for both grandfathers. Also a respectful address for any old man and a title for Alevi religious elders.
A transparent compound: anne + anne. Turkish names grandmothers by which side they are on.
Compound of baba + anne. 'Nine' is a general word for grandmother or old woman.
Father's brother; his sister is 'hala'. Also a polite address for an older man. Mother's brother is a different word, 'dayı'.
Mother's brother; her sister is 'teyze'. 'Teyze' is also the polite address for an older woman, like 'auntie'.
Gender-neutral word for husband or wife: 'eşim' = my spouse. The basic meaning is 'one of a pair, counterpart'.
'Kocam' = my husband. The feminine counterpart 'karı' (wife) can sound coarse, so 'eşim' is the polite choice for both.
Native Turkic. 'Torunum' = my grandchild.
Also 'doll'. Bebek is a well-known neighbourhood on the Bosphorus in Istanbul.
From 'arka' (back) + -daş (fellow): someone who has your back. 'Arkadaşım' = my friend. The suffix -daş also forms 'vatandaş' (citizen).
Native Turkish (from 'konmak', to settle). Neighbour relations are important in Turkish culture; 'komşuluk' is neighbourliness.
Follows the first name: 'Ahmet Bey'. The female equivalent 'hanım' works the same way: 'Ayşe Hanım'. Both are used in shops and offices.
From Arabic 'insān'. Plural 'insanlar' = people. 'Kişi' is used for counting persons: 'üç kişi' = three people.
Also the infinitive of 'ekmek' (to sow, to plant). Bread is central to every Turkish meal; 'ekmek parası' means one's livelihood.
Irregular with possessive suffixes: 'suyu' (its water), not 'susu'. 'Maden suyu' is sparkling mineral water.
From Chinese 'chá' via Persian. Black tea served in small tulip-shaped glasses is the national drink; Turkey has one of the highest per-capita tea consumptions in the world.
From Arabic 'qahwa'. The Turkish form gave European languages 'coffee', 'café', 'Kaffee'. 'Türk kahvesi' is unfiltered, brewed in a cezve.
Native Turkic. 'Sütlaç' (rice pudding) is süt + aş (food).
From Persian 'panīr'. 'Beyaz peynir' (white cheese) is the feta-like staple of breakfast.
Native Turkic. 'Menemen' is eggs scrambled with tomato and pepper.
Also means 'flesh'. Do not confuse with 'et-' the stem of etmek (to do), as in 'teşekkür ederim'.
Native Turkic. On menus 'tavuk' is chicken meat; 'piliç' is a young chicken.
'Balıkçı' is a fisherman or fish shop (suffix -çı = person who deals with). 'Balık ekmek' is Istanbul's famous fish sandwich.
From Persian 'birinj'. 'Pirinç' is raw rice; cooked rice is 'pilav'. Also means 'brass'.
From Persian 'sabza' (greenery). 'Sebzeli' = with vegetables.
From Persian 'mīva'. 'Meyve suyu' = fruit juice (literally fruit's water).
Native Turkic. 'Elma çayı' (apple tea) is a sweet drink popular with tourists.
Borrowed from Greek 'domátes', itself a plural form, so the Turkish singular ends in -s.
The ğ is silent and lengthens the o: 'so-an'. 'Sarımsak' is garlic.
From Arabic 'zaytūn'. 'Zeytinyağı' (olive oil) is zeytin + yağ + -ı.
From Persian 'shakar', related to English 'sugar'. Also means 'sweet, candy'; 'Şeker Bayramı' is the holiday ending Ramadan.
'Tuzlu' = salty, 'tuzsuz' = without salt. The suffixes -lı/-li and -sız/-siz mean 'with' and 'without'.
Native Turkic. 'Balım' (my honey) is a term of endearment; 'bal gibi' means 'just like honey', i.e. perfectly.
Yoghurt mixed with water and salt, drunk with kebab. Native Turkic word, related to 'ayırmak' (to separate), referring to the churning of butter.
One of the few Turkish words borrowed into English. From 'yoğurmak' (to knead, thicken). The ğ lengthens the vowel: 'yo-urt'.
From 'kahve' + 'altı' (under, before): the meal before coffee. Turkish breakfast is a spread of cheese, olives, eggs, bread and tea.
The infinitive 'yemek' also means 'food, meal, dish'. Stem ye- becomes yi- before -yor: yiyorum.
Also used for smoking: 'sigara içmek'. The stem iç- is identical to 'iç' (inside).
French 'restaurant' respelled phonetically, as Turkish does with all its French loans.
From Italian 'locanda' (inn). A 'lokanta' is typically a simple place serving ready-cooked home-style dishes.
French 'café' respelled. A traditional 'kahvehane' (coffee house) is a different, male-dominated institution.
French 'garçon' (boy) respelled. Used for waiters of any gender; to call one say 'Bakar mısınız?' (would you look?).
French 'menu' respelled with ü.
From Arabic 'ḥisāb' (reckoning). Also means a bank account or an online account. Final p softens: 'hesabı' (the bill).
From Persian 'bakhshish' (gift), the same word as English 'baksheesh'. Around 5-10% is customary in restaurants.
Ultimately from Latin 'mensa', the same source as Spanish 'mesa'. Also means 'desk'.
Native Turkic; also means 'forked, branching', as in 'çatal yol' (fork in the road).
Related to 'biçmek' (to cut, mow). Two dotless ı's.
Native Turkic. 'Çorba kaşığı' is a soup/table spoon, 'çay kaşığı' a teaspoon.
From Arabic 'ṭabaq'. Final k softens: 'tabağı' (the plate).
Native Turkic. 'Bir bardak su' = a glass of water. The material glass is 'cam'.

example.en: Could I have a glass of water?

note: From Arabic 'finjān'. 'Kahve fincanı' is the tiny Turkish coffee cup; 'bir fincan kahve' = a cup of coffee.
From Persian 'shīsha' (glass). 'Bir şişe su' = a bottle of water.
From Persian 'shūrbā'. 'Mercimek çorbası' (lentil soup) is on nearly every menu.
From Arabic 'kabāb'. Final p softens before a vowel: 'kebabı'. 'Adana kebap' and 'döner kebap' are named by city and by 'turning'.
Related to Greek 'pita'. A boat-shaped flatbread baked with cheese, meat or egg; also the round bread sold at Ramadan.
Layered filo pastry with cheese, spinach or mince. 'Su böreği' (water börek) is boiled first. 'Börekçi' is a börek shop.
Layered pastry with nuts and syrup. Gaziantep's pistachio baklava is protected by a geographical indication.
From Persian 'maza' (taste). Small cold dishes shared at the start of a meal, often with rakı.
Alternatively 'Hesabı alabilir miyim?' (may I get the bill?). Bills are usually brought only when asked.
'Tavsiye' (advice) is Arabic; with 'etmek' it means 'to recommend'. The -siniz ending is polite.
'Sipariş' (order) is Persian 'sifāriş'; 'vermek' is 'to give'. Many Turkish verbs are noun + vermek/etmek/olmak.
An outdoor tea place, common in parks and by the sea. Noun compounds take the possessive -(s)i on the second word: çay bahçe-si.
'Sağa' = to the right (dative -a). The same word means 'alive, healthy', as in 'sağ ol' (thanks).
'Sola' = to the left, 'solda' = on the left. Also 'left-wing' in politics.
'Düz gidin' = go straight. The basic meaning is 'flat, even, smooth'; 'düzgün' means proper, neat.
Takes the dative: 'otele yakın' = near the hotel. 'Yakında' means both 'nearby' and 'soon'.
Related to 'uzun' (long). 'Buradan uzak mı?' = Is it far from here? 'Uzak Doğu' is the Far East.

example.en: Is the museum far from here?

note: From Arabic 'kharīṭa'. 'Haritada göster' = show (it) on the map.
French 'billet' respelled. 'Gidiş dönüş bileti' = return ticket (going-returning ticket).
French 'passeport' respelled. 'Pasaport kontrolü' = passport control.
Compound of 'hava' (air, Arabic) + 'liman' (harbour, Greek) + possessive -ı. 'Havaalanı' (air field) is an older synonym.
French 'hôtel' respelled; the silent h is dropped. 'Otelde kalıyorum' = I'm staying at a hotel.
Native Turkic. 'Yolculuk' = journey, 'yolcu' = traveller. 'İyi yolculuklar' = have a good trip.
From Persian 'gūsha'. 'Köşede' = at the corner; 'köşeyi dönün' = turn the corner.
'Bankanın karşısında' = opposite the bank. Also 'against': 'buna karşı' = against this.
'İleride' = further ahead. From 'il-' (front) with the same -eri ending as 'geri' (back) and 'dışarı' (outside).
'Geri dön' = go back. 'Geri' also means 'backward' in the sense of underdeveloped.
'Bu' (this) + 'ara' (place) + locative -da. Colloquially shortened to 'burda'. 'Buraya' = to here, 'buradan' = from here.

example.en: I want to get off here.

note: 'O' (that) + 'ara' + -da. 'Şurada' is 'just there' (pointing). The three-way bu/şu/o distinction is like this/that/yonder.
The final t of the stem softens to d before a vowel: gidiyorum. Destination takes the dative: 'İstanbul'a gidiyorum'.

example.en: We are going to Ankara tomorrow.

note: Means both 'to turn' and 'to come back'. 'Döner' (the rotating kebab) is its aorist participle: 'that which turns'.
'Kayıp' (lost, Arabic) + 'olmak' (to become), written as one word with the vowel dropped. 'Kayboldum' = I'm lost.
From Arabic 'siyāḥa'. 'Seyahat etmek' = to travel; 'seyahat acentesi' = travel agency. 'Yolculuk' is the native synonym.
From Arabic 'taʿṭīl' (suspension of work). 'Tatildeyim' = I'm on holiday; 'yaz tatili' = summer holiday.

example.en: We went to Bodrum on holiday.

note: 'Tuvalet' is French 'toilette'; 'nerede' = where (at). Turkish puts the question word where the answer would go, so no inversion is needed.
From 'af' (pardon, Arabic ʿafw) + 'etmek', in the aorist 'you (polite)' form. The usual way to stop a stranger before asking directions.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

note: French 'valise' respelled. 'Bavul' (from Italian 'baule') is an older synonym.
French 'autobus' respelled with ü. 'Otobüs durağı' = bus stop; 'otogar' is the intercity bus terminal.
From Arabic 'ʿaraba' (cart). Originally any wheeled vehicle, now the everyday word for car; 'otomobil' is formal.
Respelled from French/English. Turkish taxis are yellow; 'taksimetre' is the meter.
French 'train' respelled. 'Hızlı tren' = high-speed train.
Coined in the 1930s language reform from 'uçmak' (to fly) + -ak, replacing the Ottoman 'tayyare'. 'Uçakla' = by plane.

example.en: What time does the plane take off?

note: From French 'vapeur' (steam). The Istanbul Bosphorus ferries are still called 'vapur'; 'feribot' is used for car ferries.
Native Turkic. 'Gemiyle' = by ship.
Same as French. Istanbul's 'Tünel' (1875) is one of the world's oldest underground lines.
From French 'tramway', spelled as pronounced.
French 'bicyclette' respelled. 'Bisiklete binmek' = to ride a bike (literally to mount).
Past participle of 'dolmak' (to fill up): it leaves when it is full. A fixed-route minibus; you pass your fare forward through other passengers.
From 'durmak' (to stop) + -ak. 'Bir sonraki durak' = the next stop; 'durakta' = at the stop.

example.en: I'm getting off at the next stop.

note: French 'station' respelled; Turkish adds i- before initial st-. A main railway terminus is also called 'gar' (French 'gare').
'Yaya geçidi' = pedestrian crossing. 'Yaya' also means 'on foot': 'yaya gidiyorum'.
From Italian 'scala' (ladder, landing). Also means scaffolding. Istanbul ferry stops are 'iskele'.
'Yol' (road) + -cu, the suffix for a person connected with something (also in 'işçi', 'balıkçı', 'kapıcı').
French 'chauffeur' respelled with ş and ö. Used for taxi and bus drivers; 'sürücü' is the general word.
From 'sürmek' (to drive) + -ücü. 'Sürücü belgesi' or 'ehliyet' = driving licence.
French 'trafic' respelled. 'Trafik var' = there's traffic; 'trafik ışığı' = traffic light.

example.en: There's a lot of traffic today.

note: From French 'benzine'. 'Benzin istasyonu' or 'benzinlik' = petrol station.
Used for boarding any vehicle and for riding a horse or bike. Takes the dative: 'otobüse binmek'.

en: to get off / to go down
note: The opposite of binmek; takes the ablative: 'otobüsten inmek'. Also 'to descend' and, of prices, 'to fall'.
'Araba sürmek' = to drive a car. Also means 'to last' ('iki saat sürüyor' = it takes two hours) and 'to spread, apply'.
The root of 'uçak' (plane) and 'uçuş' (flight). 'Uçurtma' (kite) is 'the thing made to fly'.
'Nereye' is 'where' with the dative -ye (to where). Compare 'nerede' (where at) and 'nereden' (where from).
From Arabic 'sāʿa'. One word for hour, o'clock, clock and watch. Takes front-vowel suffixes despite the a: 'saati', 'saatler'.
From Arabic 'daqīqa' (fine, precise). 'Bir dakika!' = just a minute!
Also 'sun' in older usage (modern 'güneş'). 'Günlük' = daily or a diary; 'gündüz' = daytime.
From Persian 'hafta', from 'haft' (seven). 'Haftaya' = next week; 'geçen hafta' = last week.
One word for both month and moon, as in many languages. 'Bu ay' = this month; 'Ay yıldız' = the crescent and star of the flag.
Native Turkic; the Arabic loan 'sene' is also common. 'Yılbaşı' (year-head) = New Year.
'Bu' (this) + 'gün' (day) fused into one word. Pronounced 'bu-gün' with the stress on the second syllable.
'Yarın görüşürüz' = see you tomorrow. 'Öbür gün' = the day after tomorrow.
'Dün akşam' = last night (yesterday evening). 'Evvelsi gün' = the day before yesterday.
'Şimdilik' = for now. 'Hemen şimdi' = right now.
From Arabic 'ṣabāḥ'. 'Sabahları' = in the mornings; 'bu sabah' = this morning. 'Sabah kahvaltısı' is the breakfast spread.
'Öğle yemeği' = lunch (noon meal); 'öğleden sonra' = afternoon (after noon).
'Akşam yemeği' = dinner; 'bu akşam' = tonight (this evening). 'Akşamüstü' is late afternoon.
'Gece yarısı' = midnight (night's half). 'Geceleri' = at night (habitually).
'Pazar' (Sunday) + 'ertesi' (the day after). Day names are lowercase in running text and capitalised only in a full date.
Day names are lowercase in running text ('salı günü') and capitalised only inside a full date. 'Salı pazarı' = Tuesday market.
From Persian 'chahār-shanba' (four + day). The suffix -şamba appears in Perşembe too.
From Persian 'panj-shanba' (five + day). Vowel harmony has turned the Persian vowels into e's.
From Arabic 'jumʿa' (gathering, assembly), the day of communal prayer. The Turkish c is always pronounced like English j.
'Cuma' + 'ertesi' (the day after), built the same way as 'pazartesi' (after Sunday).
From Persian 'bāzār' (market): Sunday was market day. 'Pazar' still means an open-air market, so 'pazar günü pazara gittim' = on Sunday I went to the market.
'Hafta' + 'son' (end) + possessive -u. 'Hafta sonunda' = at the weekend. 'Hafta içi' = weekday (week's inside).

example.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

note: A native word chosen in 1945 to replace Arabic 'Kânunusani'. Most other months keep Latin-based names: şubat, mart, nisan, mayıs, haziran, temmuz, ağustos, eylül, ekim, kasım, aralık.
Named in 1945 from 'ara' (gap) + -lık, replacing Arabic 'Kânunuevvel'. 'Ekim' (October, sowing) and 'kasım' (November) were also chosen then.
Answer with 'Saat üç' (it's three). 'Saat kaçta?' (at what time?) adds the locative -ta, answered with 'saat üçte'.
From Persian 'rang'. Final k softens before a vowel: 'rengi' (its colour). 'Renkli' = colourful; 'ne renk?' = what colour?
From Arabic 'qirmizī' (crimson, from the kermes insect dye), the same source as English 'crimson'. The older native word 'kızıl' survives in names like Kızılay (Red Crescent).
From Arabic 'māʾī' (water-coloured, from 'māʾ' = water). 'Gök' (sky) gives 'gök mavisi', sky blue.

example.en: The sea is very blue today.

note: Native Turkic, related to 'yaş' (fresh, moist). 'Yeşillik' = greenery, also salad greens.
Native Turkic. 'Sarışın' = blond (sarı + -şın). The Sarı Yer (Sarıyer) district is 'yellow place'.
From Persian 'siyāh'. The native 'kara' is also common, especially in compounds and names (Karadeniz = Black Sea).
Native Turkic for black, also meaning 'land' (as opposed to sea). Found in 'Karadeniz', 'Karaköy' and 'kara gün' (dark day).
From Arabic 'bayāḍ' (whiteness). The native 'ak' survives in 'Akdeniz' (Mediterranean, the white sea) and 'ak saçlı' (white-haired).
Older native word for white, mostly in compounds and names: Akdeniz (Mediterranean), Aksaray (white palace), 'ak akçe kara gün içindir' (white money is for a black day).
From 'turunç' (bitter orange, Persian) + -cu. The fruit orange is 'portakal', from 'Portugal'.
'Mor' covers purple and violet. 'Mor menekşe' = purple violet; 'morarmak' = to go purple (bruise).
From Persian 'panba' (cotton). 'Pembe' is also used for rosy optimism: 'pembe gözlük' = rose-tinted glasses.
Compound: 'kahve' (coffee) + 'rengi' (its colour). Many Turkish colour names are built this way: 'gül kurusu' (dried rose = dusty pink).
French 'gris' respelled. The native 'boz' is used for grey animals and in 'bozkır' (steppe).
From Persian 'lājvard' (lapis lazuli), the same root as 'azure'. Used for dark blue, e.g. school uniforms.
'Açık mavi' = light blue. The basic meaning is 'open' (from açmak, to open): 'dükkân açık' = the shop is open; also 'clear, frank'.
'Koyu kırmızı' = dark red. Also 'thick, strong': 'koyu çay' = strong tea. 'Karanlık' is dark in the sense of unlit.
From Arabic 'shakl'. The vowel drops with suffixes: 'şekli' (its shape). 'Bu şekilde' = in this way.
From Arabic 'dāʾira'. Also means 'apartment, flat' and 'office department'. 'Çember' (Persian) is the circle's outline.
From French 'carré'. 'Kare metre' = square metre. A town square is 'meydan'.
A language-reform coinage: 'üç' (three) + '-gen' (angle). Likewise 'dörtgen' (quadrilateral), 'beşgen' (pentagon), 'çokgen' (polygon).
'Dik' (upright, perpendicular) + 'dörtgen' (four-angle). A transparent modern coinage replacing Arabic 'mustatil'.
From 'yuvarlamak' (to roll). 'Yuvarlak masa' = round table; also used for round numbers.
From 'çizmek' (to draw) + -gi. 'Çizgili' = striped; 'çizgi film' = cartoon (line film).
From Arabic 'nuqṭa'. Means a dot, a point (in space or argument) and the full stop. 'Noktalı' = dotted: the i's dot distinguishes i from ı.
From Arabic 'wujūd' (existence, being). Final t softens: 'vücudu'. 'Beden' (Arabic) is a synonym used for clothing sizes.
Also 'chief, beginning, top': 'başkent' = capital (head city), 'başlamak' = to begin. 'Başım ağrıyor' = my head aches.
From Arabic 'qafā' (nape). More colloquial and physical than 'baş': 'kafam karıştı' = I'm confused (my head got mixed).
'Gözlük' = glasses (göz + -lük, the thing for eyes). 'Gözün aydın' = congratulations (may your eye be bright).
Final k softens: 'kulağım' (my ear). 'Kulaklık' = headphones (ear-thing).
The second vowel drops with suffixes: 'burnum' (my nose). Also means a cape or headland.
Vowel drops with suffixes: 'ağzım' (my mouth). Also 'dialect' and the mouth of a river or bottle.
'Dişçi' = dentist (tooth-person); 'diş fırçası' = toothbrush. 'Dişi' (with the -i) is a different word: female.
'Elim' = my hand; 'el sıkmak' = to shake hands. A different 'el' means 'stranger, other people'.
Also 'sleeve' and 'branch (of an organisation)'. 'Kolay' (easy) is unrelated.
Final k softens: 'bacağım' (my leg). Pronounced 'ba-jak' since c is always like English j.
'Ayakkabı' (shoe) is 'foot-cover'. 'Ayakta' = standing (on foot). Final k softens: 'ayağım'.
From Arabic 'qalb'. Final p softens: 'kalbim' (my heart). 'Yürek' is the native word, used more for courage and emotion.
Head hair only; body hair is 'kıl', animal fur 'tüy'. 'Saçım' = my hair; 'saç kestirmek' = to get a haircut.
From Arabic 'miʿda'. 'Midem bulanıyor' = I feel nauseous (my stomach is getting cloudy).
'Sırt çantası' = backpack (back bag). 'Sırtım ağrıyor' = my back hurts. 'Arka' is 'back' in the sense of rear side.
From French 'docteur'. The Arabic-derived 'hekim' is also used, as in 'aile hekimi' (family doctor).

example.en: I need to go to the doctor.

note: 'Hasta' (sick) + Persian '-hane' (house), with the h dropped. Same pattern as 'eczane', 'kütüphane' (library), 'postane' (post office).
Arabic 'ecza' (drugs, ingredients) + Persian '-hane' (house). Look for the red E sign; 'nöbetçi eczane' is the duty pharmacy open at night.
From Arabic 'ʿilāj' (treatment). Final ç softens: 'ilacı'. 'İlaç almak' = to take medicine.
From Persian 'khasta' (wounded, weary). Both adjective and noun: 'hastayım' = I'm ill; 'hasta' = a patient.
'Sağ' (alive, healthy) + -lık, the suffix that makes abstract nouns. 'Sağlıklı' = healthy; 'Sağlık Bakanlığı' = Ministry of Health.
From Persian 'ātash' (fire). 'Ateşim var' = I have a fever. 'Ateş etmek' = to shoot.
'Dinlenmek' (to rest) and 'dinlemek' (to listen) look alike; the extra -n- marks the difference. 'Dinlenme tesisi' = roadside rest area.

example.en: I need to rest a little.

note: Pattern for any pain: body part + -(i)m (my) + 'ağrıyor' (aches). 'Ağrı' is pain; 'ağrı kesici' = painkiller (pain cutter).
'Evde' = at home, 'eve' = (to) home, 'evim' = my house. 'Ev hanımı' = housewife; 'ev sahibi' = host or landlord (house owner).

example.en: I'm at home in the evening.

note: Native Turkic. 'Tek kişilik oda' = single room; 'oda arkadaşı' = roommate.
From Arabic 'maṭbakh' (place of cooking). Final k softens: 'mutfağa' (to the kitchen). 'Türk mutfağı' = Turkish cuisine.
From Italian 'bagno'. Also means 'a bath': 'banyo yapmak' = to take a bath. The toilet is usually separate: 'tuvalet'.
Noun + noun compounds take the possessive on the second word: yatak oda-sı. Likewise 'çocuk odası' (children's room), 'oturma odası' (sitting room).
From French 'salon'. The formal reception room of a Turkish home; 'oturma odası' is the everyday sitting room.
'Kapıcı' = doorman/caretaker of a block of flats (kapı + -cı). 'Kapıyı kapat' = close the door.
From Persian 'panjara'. 'Pencereyi aç' = open the window. 'Cam' (glass) is often used colloquially for a window pane.
From 'yatmak' (to lie down) + -ak. 'Yatağa gitmek' = to go to bed; final k softens to ğ.
The original meaning 'armpit' still exists: 'koltuk altı'. Also a seat in a theatre or plane, and a post or position of power.
Compound of 'buz' (ice) + 'dolap' (cupboard) + possessive -ı. Written as one word. 'Derin dondurucu' = freezer (deep freezer).

example.en: The milk is in the fridge.

note: From Arabic 'dūlāb' (wheel, water wheel). Final p softens: 'dolabı'. 'Dolap çevirmek' (to turn a wheel) means to scheme.
From Greek 'anoikhtári' (opener). 'Anahtarım nerede?' = where is my key? Also used for 'key' in music and computing.
From Greek 'lámpa'. 'Lambayı yak' = turn on the lamp (literally: light it), 'lambayı söndür' = turn it off (extinguish).
Coined in the late 1960s from 'bilgi' (knowledge, information) + 'sayar' (that which counts), and it completely replaced the loan 'kompüter'.
'Telefon etmek' or 'aramak' = to phone. 'Cep telefonu' (pocket phone) = mobile phone.
French 'télévision' respelled with -zyon. 'Televizyon izlemek' = to watch TV.
From Persian 'bāghcha', diminutive of 'bāgh' (garden). 'Bahçeli ev' = house with a garden; 'çay bahçesi' = tea garden.
French 'balcon' respelled. 'Balkonda oturmak' (sitting on the balcony) is a favourite summer evening activity.
From Persian 'dīvār'. 'Duvarda' = on the wall. 'Çin Seddi' (Great Wall) uses the Arabic 'sed' instead.
'Temiz' (clean, Arabic) + -le-, the suffix that makes verbs from nouns and adjectives. 'Temizlik' = cleaning, cleanliness.
'Uyku' = sleep (noun); 'uyanmak' = to wake up. 'İyi uykular' = sleep well.
For washing things and people; 'yıkanmak' (reflexive -n-) = to wash oneself. 'Bulaşık yıkamak' = to wash the dishes.
From Arabic 'kirāʾ'. 'Kiralık' = for rent (sign on buildings); 'kiracı' = tenant; 'kiralamak' = to rent.
From Persian 'āyina'. 'Aynaya bakmak' = to look in the mirror.
From Arabic 'albisa', plural of 'libās' (garment). Means a woman's dress, and in the plural 'elbiseler', clothes in general.
Native Turkic. Final k softens: 'gömleği'. Also the slough of a snake.
French 'pantalon' respelled. Singular in Turkish: 'bir pantolon' = a pair of trousers.
Also 'the lower edge' of anything: 'dağın eteği' = the foot of the mountain. Final k softens: 'eteği'.
From French 'jaquette', with the c pronounced like English j. A suit is 'takım elbise' (set of clothes).
The everyday word for a padded or sporty outdoor jacket. 'Kaban' is a heavier short coat.
From French 'paletot'. A long, formal winter coat.
Same spelling as 'Kazak' (Kazakh / Cossack); the garment is said to be named after a Cossack-style tunic. Final k softens: 'kazağım'.
English 'T-shirt' spelled exactly as Turks pronounce it, with ş and ö. A good example of Turkish phonetic spelling of loanwords.
'Ayak' (foot) + 'kap' (cover, container) + -ı. Note the double k. Shoes come off at the door of every Turkish home.
From Persian 'jūrāb'. Final p softens: 'çorabım'. 'Külotlu çorap' = tights.
A Slavic loan (Russian 'shapka'). The 1925 Hat Law made the brimmed hat replace the fez for men.
From Arabic 'qiyāfa'. 'Kıyafet' is clothing as an outfit or dress code; 'giysi' is the native synonym from giymek.
From 'atmak' (to throw) + -kı. A woollen scarf; a woman's headscarf is 'başörtüsü' or 'eşarp' (French écharpe).
Begins with 'el' (hand). Usually plural: 'eldivenler'; 'bir çift eldiven' = a pair of gloves.
From Persian 'kamar' (waist). Also 'arch' in architecture and 'seat belt' ('emniyet kemeri').
Any bag: handbag, schoolbag, briefcase. 'Sırt çantası' = backpack; 'el çantası' = handbag.
From Persian 'juzdān' (document holder). Also 'nüfus cüzdanı', the old ID card. Pronounced 'jüzdan'.
'Göz' (eye) + -lük, the suffix for 'thing meant for'. 'Güneş gözlüğü' = sunglasses. 'Gözlükçü' = optician.
From Arabic 'badan' (body). 'Kaç beden?' = what size? Shoe size is 'numara' instead.
For clothes on the body. Hats and glasses use 'takmak' (to attach), shoes can use 'giymek'. 'Giyinmek' = to get dressed.

en: to take off / to take out
note: Causative of 'çıkmak' (to go out). Used for removing clothes, taking things out of a bag, and even publishing.
'Deneyebilir miyim?' = may I try it on? Stem vowel e becomes i before -yor: deniyorum. 'Deneme' = an essay or a trial.
Every Turkish home has guest slippers by the door. 'Terlik' is singular for the pair; 'plaj terliği' = flip-flops.
'İç' (inside) + 'çamaşır' (laundry, Persian) + -ı. 'Çamaşır yıkamak' = to do the laundry; 'çamaşır makinesi' = washing machine.
'İşim var' = I'm busy (I have work). 'İş yeri' = workplace; 'iş adamı' = businessman. Capital İ keeps its dot.
'İş' + -çi, the agent suffix (-cı/-ci/-cu/-cü, with ç after voiceless consonants). 'İşçi Bayramı' = Labour Day.
A 1930s reform coinage from 'okumak' (to read, study), chosen partly for its resemblance to French 'école'. It replaced Arabic 'mektep'.
From 'öğrenmek' (to learn) + -ci. A reform coinage replacing Arabic 'talebe'. 'Öğrenci kartı' = student card.
From 'öğretmek' (to teach) + -men. Replaced Arabic 'muallim' after the language reform. 'Öğretmenler Günü' is 24 November.
French 'université' respelled. 'Üniversitede okuyorum' = I study at university (literally: I read).
From Arabic 'dars'. 'Ders çalışmak' = to study (for lessons); 'Türkçe dersi' = Turkish lesson; 'ders almak' = to learn a lesson.
From Arabic 'kitāb'. Final p softens: 'kitabım' (my book). 'Kitapçı' = bookshop; 'kitaplık' = bookcase.
From Arabic 'qalam' (reed pen), ultimately Greek 'kálamos'. 'Kurşun kalem' (lead pen) = pencil; 'tükenmez kalem' (never-ending pen) = ballpoint.
From Arabic 'daftar', ultimately Greek 'diphthéra' (hide, parchment). 'Not defteri' = notebook; 'defterdar' was an Ottoman treasurer.
Reform coinage from 'sınamak' (to test), replacing Arabic 'imtihan', which is still heard. 'Sınava girmek' = to sit an exam (enter).
From French/English 'office'. 'Büro' (French 'bureau') is also common; 'ofiste' = at the office.
From 'toplanmak' (to gather) + -tı. 'Toplantıdayım' = I'm in a meeting; 'toplantı odası' = meeting room.
From French 'patron'. 'Müdür' (Arabic) is a manager or director; 'şef' (French 'chef') is a section head.
From Arabic 'maʿāsh' (means of living). 'Maaş almak' = to be paid; 'asgari ücret' = minimum wage.
From Arabic 'maslak' (path). 'Mesleğiniz ne?' = what is your profession? Final k softens to ğ.
From Arabic 'muhandis' (geometer, from 'handasa' = geometry). A prestigious title in Turkey, often used before the name.
From French 'avocat' respelled. 'Avukat tutmak' = to hire a lawyer.
From Persian 'hamshīra' (sister, literally 'same milk'). Used for nurses of either sex, like English 'sister' on a hospital ward.
Means both 'to work' and 'to study hard'. 'Nerede çalışıyorsun?' = where do you work? 'Çalışkan' = hard-working.
'To read' and also 'to be a student': 'üniversitede okuyorum'. Originally 'to call out', hence 'okul' (school) and 'okur' (reader).
'Yazı' = writing, article; 'yazar' = writer; 'yazılım' = software. 'Yaz' alone also means 'summer'.
'Türkçe öğreniyorum' = I'm learning Turkish. The -n- is the reflexive: to teach oneself; 'öğretmek' is the causative 'to teach'.
Causative -t- on the same root as öğrenmek. 'Öğretmen' = teacher; 'öğretim' = instruction.
'Anlamıyorum' = I don't understand; 'anladım' = I got it. The noun 'anlam' = meaning. Stem vowel a drops before -ıyor: anlıyorum.

example.en: I don't understand, could you repeat?

note: From Arabic 'hawāʾ'. 'Hava nasıl?' = what's the weather like? 'Hava güzel' = it's nice out. Also air: 'temiz hava' = fresh air.
Related to 'gün' (day). 'Güneşli' = sunny; 'güneş kremi' = sunscreen.
From 'yağmak' (to fall as precipitation). 'Yağmur yağıyor' = it's raining (rain is falling). 'Yağmurluk' = raincoat.
'Kar yağıyor' = it's snowing. A different word 'kâr' (with a circumflex, from Persian) means profit.

example.en: There is snow in the mountains.

note: From Persian 'rūzgār' (time, fortune). The circumflex marks a long â and is often dropped: 'rüzgar'. 'Rüzgârlı' = windy.
Native Turkic. 'Bulutlu' = cloudy. Also used for cloud computing.
'Hava sıcak' = it's hot. For people feeling hot: 'sıcaktan bunaldım'. 'Sıcaklık' = temperature. Three dotless ı's in a row to practise.
'Hava soğuk' = it's cold; 'üşüyorum' = I'm cold (I'm feeling chilled). 'Soğuk' also describes an unfriendly person.
Between sıcak and soğuk: 'ılık su' = lukewarm water, 'ılık bir gün' = a mild day. Starts with a dotless ı.
'Denize girmek' = to go for a swim (enter the sea). A popular name for both boys and girls. 'Akdeniz' = Mediterranean, 'Karadeniz' = Black Sea.
The ğ lengthens the a: 'daa'. 'Dağlar' = mountains; 'Ağrı Dağı' = Mount Ararat.
From Arabic 'nahr'. The vowel drops with suffixes: 'nehri'. 'Irmak' is the native synonym, as in Kızılırmak (red river).
Native Turkic. 'Van Gölü' = Lake Van; 'Tuz Gölü' = the Salt Lake.
'Ormanda' = in the forest. 'Orman yangını' = forest fire.
Final ç softens: 'ağacı'. 'Ağaçlık' = woodland; 'zeytin ağacı' = olive tree.
Final k softens: 'çiçeği'. 'Çiçekçi' = florist. Tulips ('lale') came to Europe from Ottoman gardens.
'Gök' (sky) + 'kuşak' (belt, sash) + -ı, one word. The k of kuşak softens to ğ before the suffix.
'Gök' (sky, also an old word for blue) + 'yüz' (face) + -ü. 'Gök gürültüsü' = thunder (sky's rumbling).
Native Turkic. The star on the flag; also a celebrity. A common girl's name.
From Arabic 'ḥayawān'. 'Hayvanat bahçesi' = zoo (animals' garden). Also an insult, as in English 'beast'.
Istanbul's street cats are famous. 'Kedi' is likely of the same ultimate origin as English 'cat' and Latin 'cattus'.
Final k softens: 'köpeği'. 'Köpek balığı' (dog fish) = shark.
'Kuşlar' = birds. 'Kuş bakışı' = bird's-eye view. 'Kuşadası' (bird island) is a resort town.
Used only with rain, snow, hail: 'yağmur yağıyor', 'kar yağıyor'. Only third-person forms are normally used.
'Rüzgâr esiyor' = the wind is blowing. 'Esinti' = breeze. Also idiomatic: 'aklına esmek' = to take it into one's head.
From Persian 'pāra' (piece, fragment), originally a small Ottoman coin. 'Param yok' = I have no money. 'Para' is also the currency name in several Balkan languages.
From Italian 'lira' (ultimately Latin 'libra', pound). The symbol ₺ was adopted in 2012. '100 lira' is written '100 TL'.
From German 'Groschen', via Ottoman trade with Europe. 'Beş kuruş etmez' = not worth five kuruş (worthless).
'Fiyatı ne kadar?' = what is its price? 'Fiyat listesi' = price list. Of Arabic origin.
Native Turkic. 'Daha ucuz' = cheaper; 'ucuzluk' = a sale (cheapness).
From Persian 'bahā' (price) + -lı (with). 'Çok pahalı!' = too expensive!

example.target: Bu çok pahalı, daha ucuzu var mı?
example.en: This is too expensive, is there a cheaper one?

note: From Arabic 'makhāzin' (storehouses), the same source as English 'magazine' and French 'magasin'. The ğ lengthens the a.
From Arabic 'dukkān'. The circumflex shows the k is palatalised ('kyan'); often written 'dükkan'. 'Bakkal' is the corner grocery.
From English 'market', but it means a self-service grocery shop, not a marketplace. 'Süpermarket' is the big one.
From Persian 'chārsū' (four directions, crossroads). 'Kapalıçarşı' = the Grand Bazaar (covered bazaar). 'Çarşıya gitmek' = to go shopping downtown.
From Italian 'cassa'. Also 'safe' and 'crate'. 'Kasiyer' = cashier.
From 'indirmek' (to lower, causative of inmek) + -im. 'İndirimde' = on sale; 'yüzde elli indirim' = 50% off.
'Kredi kartı' = credit card; 'kartla' = by card. 'Kartvizit' (French 'carte de visite') = business card.
From Arabic 'naqd'. 'Nakit mi, kart mı?' = cash or card? Final t softens: 'nakdi'.
From 'almak' (to take) + 'vermek' (to give): an exchange. 'Alışveriş yapmak' = to shop; 'alışveriş merkezi' (AVM) = shopping mall.
From Arabic 'hadiyya'. 'Hediye etmek' = to give as a present. 'Armağan' is the native synonym.
'Kadar' (amount, extent) is Arabic 'qadr'. 'Bu ne kadar?' = how much is this? 'Kaç lira?' (how many lira) is the alternative.
'Satın' (by purchase) + 'almak' (to take). In speech plain 'almak' usually suffices: 'ekmek aldım' = I bought bread.
'Satılık' = for sale (sign on cars and houses); 'satıcı' = seller. 'Satış' = a sale.
'Ödeme' = payment. The stem vowel e becomes ü before -yor by rounding harmony: ödüyorum.
From French 'fiche'. The till receipt; also an electrical plug. An invoice is 'fatura' (Italian 'fattura').
From Italian 'banca'. 'Bankamatik' is the common word for an ATM. 'Banka hesabı' = bank account.
'Bozuk' (broken, spoiled) + 'para'. 'Bozuk paranız var mı?' = do you have change? 'Para bozdurmak' = to get change / exchange currency.
'Geçmek' (to pass) is used for 'to be accepted'. The question particle 'mu' comes after the verb and harmonises with its last vowel.

en: to take / to get / to buy
note: One of the most used verbs: take, receive, buy. 'Bir çay alayım' = I'll have a tea. The noun 'alıcı' = buyer, receiver.
From 'mut' (joy) + -lu, the suffix meaning 'with, having'. 'Mutluluk' = happiness; 'mutsuz' = unhappy (-suz = without).
From 'üzülmek' (to be sad). 'Üzgünüm' = I'm sorry / I'm sad, the most common way to express sympathy.
From 'kızmak' (to get hot, to get angry), related to 'kızıl' (red). 'Sana kızgınım' = I'm angry with you. 'Sinirli' (nervy) is also common.
From 'yorulmak' (to get tired). 'Yorgunum' = I'm tired; 'yorgunluk' = tiredness.

example.en: I'm very tired, I want to sleep.

note: From 'korkmak' (to fear) + -ku. 'Korku filmi' = horror film. 'Korkunç' = terrible, frightening.
From Arabic 'ʿishq' (passionate love). 'Aşkım' = my love (as address). 'Âşık' = in love, and also a wandering folk poet.
From 'sevmek' (to love) + -gi. Broader and calmer than 'aşk': love for family, friends, country. 'Sevgilerle' = with love (letter closing).
'Sevgi' + -li. 'Sevgilim' = my darling; 'Sevgili Ayşe' = Dear Ayşe at the start of a letter. 'Sevgililer Günü' = Valentine's Day.
'Heyecan' (excitement, Arabic) + -lı. Covers both excited and nervous: 'sınavdan önce heyecanlıyım' = I'm nervous before the exam.
'Endişe' (worry) is Persian 'andīsha' (thought). 'Endişelenme' = don't worry. 'Merak etme' is the everyday alternative.
From Arabic 'sākin' (still, resident). 'Sakin ol' = calm down. 'Sakinleşmek' = to calm down (-leş- = to become).
From 'şaşmak' (to be astonished). 'Şaşırdım' = I was surprised; 'şaşırtıcı' = surprising.
From Arabic 'rāḥa' (rest). 'Rahat ol' = relax, make yourself at home. 'Rahatsız' = uncomfortable or unwell (without ease).
From 'utanmak' (to be ashamed, embarrassed) + -gaç. 'Utanıyorum' = I'm embarrassed.
'Gurur' (pride, Arabic) + -lu. Can be positive or mean arrogant. 'Seninle gurur duyuyorum' = I'm proud of you.
'Yalnızım' = I'm alone. Also an adverb meaning 'only' and a conjunction 'but'. 'Yalnızlık' = loneliness.
'Seni özledim' = I miss you (literally: I have missed you, past tense). 'Özlem' = longing, also a girl's name.
One verb for both liking and loving: 'çayı severim' = I like tea; 'seni seviyorum' = I love you. 'Sevimli' = cute, lovable.
'İstiyorum' = I want; 'ister misiniz?' = would you like? With another verb use the infinitive: 'gitmek istiyorum' = I want to go.
Takes the ablative: 'köpekten korkuyorum' = I'm afraid of dogs (from dogs). 'Korkma!' = don't be afraid, the first word of the national anthem.
'Gülümsemek' = to smile. 'Gül' alone is 'rose' (Persian), a different word. 'Güle güle' (laughing-laughing) is 'goodbye' said to the person leaving.
Stem vowel a drops before -ıyor: ağlıyorum. 'Ağlama!' = don't cry.

en: to be sad / to be upset
note: Passive-looking form of 'üzmek' (to upset). 'Üzülme' = don't be sad. 'Üzüntü' = sorrow.
'Can' (soul, life, Persian) + -ım (my) + 'sıkılmak' (to be squeezed). 'Canım' on its own is 'my dear'. 'Sıkıcı' = boring.
'Sen' (you) takes the accusative -i for a definite object. The present continuous is used, not the aorist 'severim', which would sound like a general preference.
'Ne yapıyorsun?' = what are you doing? 'Yemek yapmak' = to cook (make food). 'Yapı' = building, structure.
Rarely used alone; it turns loan nouns into verbs: 'teşekkür etmek' (to thank), 'yardım etmek' (to help), 'telefon etmek'. Stem t softens: ediyorum.

en: to be / to become / to happen
note: 'Ne oldu?' = what happened? 'Doktor olmak istiyorum' = I want to become a doctor. 'Olur' = OK (it becomes); 'olsun' = may it be.
The recipient takes the dative -e/-a: 'bana ver' = give (it) to me. Also in compounds: 'sipariş vermek' (to order), 'ders vermek' (to teach).
'Görüşmek' (to see each other, meet) and 'görünmek' (to appear) are built on it. 'Görüşürüz' = see you.
Takes the dative: 'bana bak' = look at me. Also 'to take care of': 'çocuğa bakmak'. 'Bakar mısınız?' is how you call a waiter.
'Duydun mu?' = did you hear? Also for feelings: 'gurur duymak' = to feel proud. 'Duygu' = emotion.
'Müzik dinlemek' = to listen to music; no preposition, the object takes the accusative. 'Dinleyici' = listener.
'Türkçe konuşuyor musunuz?' = do you speak Turkish? The -uş- is the reciprocal suffix: talking with one another.
'Şarkı söylemek' = to sing (say a song). The stem vowel e rounds to ü before -yor: söylüyorum. 'Demek' is used for quoting exact words.
'Bilmiyorum' = I don't know. 'Bilgi' (knowledge) and 'bilim' (science) are built on it. '-ebilmek' after a verb means 'can'.
'Düşünce' = thought; 'düşünür' = thinker. 'Bence' (in my opinion) is 'ben' + -ce.
'Bekle!' = wait! 'Bekleme salonu' = waiting room. The e before -yor becomes i: bekliyorum.
'Buldum!' = I found it! 'Buluşmak' (reciprocal) = to meet up; 'buluş' = invention.
Two everyday meanings: 'anahtarımı arıyorum' = I'm looking for my key; 'seni ararım' = I'll call you. 'Arama' = search, phone call.
Also 'to turn on' lights and devices, and 'to answer' the phone. 'Açık' = open; 'anahtar' is key, 'açacak' is a bottle opener.
Causative of 'kapanmak' (to be closed). 'Kapalı' = closed; 'Kapalıçarşı' = the covered bazaar. Also for switching off devices.
From 'baş' (head, beginning) + -la-. Takes the dative: 'işe başlamak' = to start work. Stem a drops before -ıyor: başlıyorum.
Causative of 'bitmek' (to end, run out): 'bitti' = it's finished / sold out. 'Yemeğini bitir' = finish your food.
'Erken kalkıyorum' = I get up early. Also for vehicles leaving: 'otobüs kalkıyor' = the bus is departing. 'Kahvaltı' comes before it!

example.en: I get up at seven every day.

note: 'Oturun' = sit down (polite). Also 'to reside': 'Kadıköy'de oturuyorum' = I live in Kadıköy. 'Oturma odası' = sitting room.
'Yürüyüş' = a walk, hike, also a protest march. 'Yürüyerek' = on foot (by walking).
'Koşu' = a run, race. 'Koş!' = run! Also 'to harness, put to work'.
Intransitive: 'uyandım' = I woke up. To wake someone else is the causative 'uyandırmak'. 'Uyanık' = awake, also 'sharp, streetwise'.
'Yardım' (help, Turkic) + 'etmek'. The person helped takes the dative: 'bana yardım eder misiniz?' = could you help me? 'İmdat!' is the cry for help.
'Bu ne?' = what is this? Builds many question words: 'neden' (why, from-what), 'ne zaman' (when), 'ne kadar' (how much), 'nerede' (where).
'Kim o?' = who is it? Takes case suffixes like a noun: 'kimin' (whose), 'kime' (to whom), 'kiminle' (with whom).
'Ne' + 're' (place) + locative -de. 'Nereye' = where to, 'nereden' = where from, 'nereli' = from where (origin). Often shortened to 'nerde'.
'Zaman' (time) is Arabic 'zamān'. Two words: 'Ne zaman geliyorsun?' = when are you coming?
'Nasılsın?' = how are you? 'Nasıl yani?' = how do you mean? 'Nasıl bir ...' = what kind of ...
'Ne' + ablative -den. Also a noun: 'neden' = reason, cause. 'Niçin' (ne için = for what) and 'niye' are synonyms.
The noun after it stays singular: 'kaç kişi?' = how many people? 'Kaç yaşındasın?' = how old are you? 'Kaçta?' = at what time?
'Hangi otobüs?' = which bus? 'Hangisi?' = which one? Of Persian origin, related to 'kangı' in older Turkish.
From Arabic 'wa'. Pure Turkish often avoids it, using 'ile' (with) or the suffix -(y)le: 'çay ile kahve' / 'çayla kahve' = tea and coffee.
From Arabic 'ammā'. 'Fakat' (Arabic) and 'ancak' (Turkic) are more formal synonyms.
Arabic 'wa' (and) + 'yā' (or). 'Ya da' is the colloquial synonym; 'yoksa' is used in questions: 'çay mı yoksa kahve mi?'
From Persian 'chūn-ki'. Starts the clause giving the reason, as in English. Note the ü in both syllables.

example.en: I didn't come because I was ill.

note: Follows the noun: 'arkadaşım ile'. Usually attached as a suffix -(y)le/-(y)la: 'arkadaşımla' (with my friend), 'otobüsle' (by bus).
A postposition: it comes after the word. 'Senin için' = for you; 'bunun için' = for this reason. Pronouns take the genitive before it.
'Çok güzel' = very beautiful; 'çok para' = a lot of money; 'çok teşekkürler' = thanks a lot. 'Çoğu' = most of.
'Biraz' (bir + az) = a little: 'biraz Türkçe' = a little Turkish. 'Az önce' = just now; 'en az' = at least.
From Persian 'hīch' (nothing). With a negative verb: 'hiç bilmiyorum' = I don't know at all. 'Hiçbir şey' = nothing; 'hiç kimse' = nobody.
From Persian 'har'. 'Her gün' = every day; 'her şey' = everything; 'herkes' = everyone; 'her zaman' = always.
Usually dropped because the verb ending shows the person; used for emphasis. Irregular dative 'bana' (to me). 'Benim' = my/mine; 'bence' = in my opinion.
Irregular dative 'sana' (to you). The polite/plural form is 'siz'; 'siz' is used with strangers, elders and in shops.
One pronoun for he, she and it: Turkish has no gender. Also the demonstrative 'that'. With suffixes it gains an n: 'onu' (him/her/it), 'onlar' (they), 'onun' (his/her/its).
Written separately after the word questioned and harmonising with it: mı/mi/mu/mü. 'Çay mı?' = tea? 'Geliyor musun?' = are you coming?
Also expresses 'have': 'param var' = I have money (my money exists). 'Var mı?' = is there? 'Varlık' = existence, wealth.
The opposite of 'var'. 'Param yok' = I have no money. Also a casual 'no' and the answer to 'var mı?'. 'Yoksa' = otherwise, or.
A separate word after the item it stresses, harmonising de/da: 'ben de' = me too. Never written joined, unlike the locative suffix -de ('evde' = at home).
Also 'great, elder': 'büyükanne' = grandmother, 'büyükbaba' = grandfather. Final k softens: 'büyüğü'.

example.en: Istanbul is a very big city.

note: Also 'little, young': 'küçük kardeş' = younger sibling. Adjectives never change for number or case in Turkish.
'Uzun boylu' = tall (long-statured) for people. 'Uzun zamandır' = for a long time.
Demonstratives: 'bu' (this), 'şu' (that, nearby or pointed at), 'o' (that, over there). Gains an n with suffixes: 'bunu' (this, acc.), 'bunlar' (these).
'Kısa boylu' = short (of people); 'kısaca' = briefly. 'Kısa kol' = short sleeve.
'İyi ki' = it's good that, luckily. 'Daha iyi' = better; 'en iyi' = best. Comparison is done with 'daha' (more) and 'en' (most).
'Kötü değil' = not bad. 'Fena' (Arabic) is a common synonym: 'fena değil'.
Far wider than 'beautiful': nice weather, tasty food, a good idea, a pretty person. 'Güzellik' = beauty; 'güzelce' = nicely.
Also 'nasty, unseemly' of behaviour. 'Çirkinlik' = ugliness.
'Yeni yıl' = new year; 'yeniden' = again (from new); 'yenilik' = novelty, innovation.
For objects and former things: 'eski araba' = old car, 'eski eşim' = my ex. For old people use 'yaşlı'. 'Eskiden' = formerly.
Also a noun: 'gençler' = young people. 'Gençlik' = youth. Final ç softens: 'genci'.
'Yaş' (age; also 'wet') + -lı. 'Kaç yaşındasın?' = how old are you (in how many years are you)? 'Yaşlılar' = the elderly.
'Kolay gelsin' (may it come easy) is said to anyone working. 'Kolayca' = easily; 'kolaylık' = convenience.
From Persian 'zūr' (force, strength). 'Zorla' = by force; 'zorluk' = difficulty; 'zorunda' = obliged to.
'Hız' (speed) + -lı. 'Hızlı tren' = high-speed train. 'Çabuk' is 'quick' in the sense of 'hurry up'.
'Yavaş yavaş' = slowly, gradually; doubling a word is a common Turkish way to make an adverb. 'Daha yavaş, lütfen' = slower, please.
From Arabic 'tamyīz' (distinction, purity). 'Temiz hava' = fresh air; 'tertemiz' = spotless (intensive doubling of the first syllable).
'Kir' (dirt) + -li. 'Kirli çamaşır' = dirty laundry. 'Pis' (Persian) is a stronger synonym: filthy.
'Tat' (taste) + -lı. Also the noun for dessert: 'tatlı ister misiniz?' And 'cute, sweet' of people. 'Tatlı su' = fresh (not salt) water.
'Acı biber' = hot pepper; 'acı kahve' = bitter coffee; as a noun, 'acı' = pain, grief. 'Acı mı?' asks if a dish is spicy.
'Lezzet' (flavour, Arabic) + -li. 'Çok lezzetli!' is the compliment to give; 'nefis' (Arabic) is a strong synonym.
A language-reform coinage from 'ilgi' (interest) + -nç, replacing Arabic 'enteresan' (itself from French). Both are heard today.
'Önem' (importance, reform coinage from 'ön' = front) + -li. 'Önemli değil' = it doesn't matter / no problem.
'Doğru mu?' = is that right? Also a postposition 'towards': 'eve doğru' = towards home. 'Doğrusu' = to tell the truth.
From 'yanılmak' (to err). 'Yanlış numara' = wrong number; 'yanlış anladım' = I misunderstood.
From Persian 'shahr'. The vowel drops with suffixes: 'şehri', 'şehrin'. 'Şehir merkezi' = city centre. 'Eskişehir' = old city.

example.en: Which city do you live in?

note: An old Central Asian loan (seen in Taşkent, Semerkant) revived in the language reform as an alternative to Persian 'şehir'. 'Kentsel' = urban.
'Köylü' = villager, peasant. Many place names end in -köy: Kadıköy, Arnavutköy, Bakırköy.
From Arabic 'maḥalla'. The basic unit of Turkish urban life, with its own 'muhtar' (elected head). 'Mahalle bakkalı' = the local corner shop.
From Arabic 'zuqāq' (lane). A small street; a main road is 'cadde'. Final k softens: 'sokağa' (to the street). 'Sokak kedisi' = street cat.
From Arabic 'jādda'. 'İstiklal Caddesi' is Istanbul's famous pedestrian street. Pronounced 'jad-de' with a double d.
From Arabic 'maydān' (open field). 'Taksim Meydanı' = Taksim Square. 'Meydan okumak' = to challenge (read the square).
'Galata Köprüsü' = the Galata Bridge; 'Boğaz Köprüsü' = the Bosphorus Bridge. Note the possessive -sü on the second word of the compound.
From Arabic 'jāmiʿ' (that which gathers). Takes an extra -i with suffixes: 'camii' (Sultanahmet Camii). Pronounced 'ja-mi'. A small mosque is 'mescit'.
From Greek 'ekklēsía'. Istanbul's Aya Sofya and Kariye were churches before becoming mosques and museums.
French 'musée' respelled. 'Müze kart' is the museum pass; 'Müzeler Günü' = Museum Day.
Also 'car park' and 'parking': 'park etmek' = to park; 'park yeri' = parking space; 'Park yapılmaz' = no parking.
French 'plage' respelled with j. 'Plaja gitmek' = to go to the beach. 'Sahil' (Arabic) is the coast or seafront promenade.
'Posta' (Italian) + Persian '-hane' (house). The Turkish post is 'PTT'. Same pattern as 'hastane' and 'eczane'.
Arabic 'kutub' (books, plural of 'kitāb') + Persian '-hane' (house). A bookshop is 'kitapçı', a bookcase 'kitaplık'.
From Arabic 'ḥammām' (bath). Also the bathroom in older houses. 'Hamam böceği' (bath beetle) = cockroach.
From Persian 'sarāy' (mansion, inn), the source of 'caravanserai' and 'seraglio'. 'Topkapı Sarayı' = Topkapı Palace.
From Arabic 'qalʿa'. Also 'goal' in football and 'rook' in chess. 'Kaleci' = goalkeeper.
From Arabic 'markaz'. 'Şehir merkezi' = city centre; 'alışveriş merkezi' = shopping mall. 'Merkezi' = central.

example.en: How can I get to the centre?

note: From Arabic 'bināʾ'. 'Apartman' (French) is a block of flats; a single flat is 'daire'.
French 'police' respelled. Means both the force and one officer: 'bir polis' = a police officer. Emergency number: 112.
From Arabic 'baladiyya' (from 'balad' = town). 'Belediye başkanı' = mayor; 'belediye otobüsü' = municipal bus.
'Adalar' (the Islands) are the Princes' Islands off Istanbul. 'Kuşadası' = bird island; 'yarımada' = peninsula (half island).
From 'yaş' (age, life). 'Nerede yaşıyorsun?' = where do you live? 'Yaşam' or 'hayat' (Arabic) = life. 'Yaşasın!' = long live! / hooray!
'Karşıya geçmek' = to cross (to the other side). Also of time: 'zaman geçiyor'. 'Geçmiş' = the past; 'geçit' = passage.
